modules.summary: Module 1 builds the foundational ability to recognise, define, and verify arithmetic progressions from both real-world contexts and lists of numbers. Segment M1.S1 establishes the formal definition of an AP — including the common difference d and the general form a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d, … — by first examining everyday sequences such as salary increments and savings deposits. Segment M1.S2 develops the skill of testing whether any given list is an AP by checking whether aₖ₊₁ − aₖ is constant across all consecutive pairs, and extends this to classifying real-world situations and writing AP terms when a and d are given. The unifying mathematical insight is that an AP is completely determined by just two numbers — its first term a and its common difference d — and that every subsequent term is generated by a single, repeating additive step. This two-parameter structure underpins all subsequent work with the nth term formula and the sum formula in later modules.

topics.summary: Arithmetic progressions are introduced through real-world sequences — salary increments, ladder rungs, and savings deposits — to build intuition that some sequences grow by a constant addition at every step, while others (geometric growth, squared numbers) do not, by computing consecutive differences across several examples.
topics.topic_name: Real-World Patterns and Introduction to Arithmetic Progressions
topics.brief_summary: Real-world sequences such as Reena's salary and Shakila's savings are used to identify which lists have a constant consecutive difference, introducing the idea of an arithmetic progression before any formal definition.
topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: Consider the chairs in a school auditorium — 15 seats in the front row, 18 in the second, 21 in the third, with exactly 3 more in each row than the one before it. You can determine the number of chairs in any row directly, without counting from the beginning, because the increment is always the same fixed value. Nature and daily life contain many sequences governed by this kind of constant, predictable change.

RECALL: In earlier classes, you encountered patterns in which numbers grow by multiplication or by forming squares. In this chapter, we focus specifically on sequences where consecutive terms always differ by the same fixed number.

You must have observed that in nature, many things follow a certain pattern, such as the petals of a sunflower, the holes of a honeycomb, the grains on a maize cob, the spirals on a pineapple and on a pine cone, etc.

We now look for some patterns which occur in our day-to-day life. Some such examples are:

(i) Reena applied for a job and got selected. She has been offered a job with a starting monthly salary of ₹ 8000, with an annual increment of ₹ 500 in her salary. Her salary (in ₹) for the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, . . . years will be, respectively

8000, 8500, 9000, . . . .

(ii) The lengths of the rungs of a ladder decrease uniformly by 2 cm from bottom to top (see Fig. 5.1). The bottom rung is 45 cm in length. The lengths (in cm) of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, . . ., 8th rung from the bottom to the top are, respectively

45, 43, 41, 39, 37, 35, 33, 31

(iii) In a savings scheme, the amount becomes 5/4 times of itself after every 3 years. The maturity amount (in ₹) of an investment of ₹ 8000 after 3, 6, 9 and 12 years will be, respectively:

10000, 12500, 15625, 19531.25

(iv) The number of unit squares in squares with side 1, 2, 3, . . . units (see Fig. 5.2) are, respectively

1², 2², 3², . . . .

(v) Shakila puts ₹ 100 into her daughter's money box when she was one year old and increased the amount by ₹ 50 every year. The amounts of money (in ₹) in the box on the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, . . . birthday were

100, 150, 200, 250, . . ., respectively.

(vi) A pair of rabbits are too young to produce in their first month. In the second, and every subsequent month, they produce a new pair. Each new pair of rabbits produce a new pair in their second month and in every subsequent month (see Fig. 5.3). Assuming no rabbit dies, the number of pairs of rabbits at the start of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, . . ., 6th month, respectively are:

1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8

In the examples above, we observe some patterns. In some, we find that the succeeding terms are obtained by adding a fixed number, in other by multiplying with a fixed number, in another we find that they are squares of consecutive numbers, and so on.

In this chapter, we shall discuss one of these patterns in which succeeding terms are obtained by adding a fixed number to the preceding terms. We shall also see how to find their nth terms and the sum of n consecutive terms, and use this knowledge in solving some daily life problems.

ERROR ALERT: A common misconception is that any increasing sequence must add a fixed number at every step. In example (iii), the amounts ₹ 10000, ₹ 12500, ₹ 15625, ₹ 19531.25 increase at every step, but the increments are ₹ 2500, ₹ 3125, and ₹ 3906.25 — growing values, because the scheme multiplies by 5/4 at each step rather than adding a constant. In example (iv), the differences between consecutive square numbers are 3, 5, 7, 9 — also not constant. Only sequences with an identical difference at every consecutive step belong to the family we study in this chapter.

CHECK: For each of the six examples above, calculate the difference between consecutive terms and identify which sequences maintain a constant difference throughout, and which do not.

concept_bullets: A sequence has a constant consecutive difference when every term is obtained by adding the same fixed number to the one before — for example, 8000, 8500, 9000 each differ by +500.
Not every increasing sequence is an AP — for example, 10000, 12500, 15625 increases at each step but the differences are 2500, 3125, and 3906.25, which are not equal.
A decreasing AP has a constant negative addition at every step — for example, 45, 43, 41, 39 each differ by −2 cm.
Squares of consecutive integers 1², 2², 3², … have differences 3, 5, 7, … which grow, so they do not form an AP.

recall_questions.answer: The sequence studied is called an Arithmetic Progression (AP). The property every AP must satisfy is: the difference between any two consecutive terms is always the same fixed number, called the common difference d.
recall_questions.prompt: Name the type of sequence studied in this chapter and state the one property that every such sequence must satisfy.

recall_questions.answer:
Sequence A is an AP. The consecutive differences are: 8500 − 8000 = 500, 9000 − 8500 = 500, 9500 − 9000 = 500. The difference is constant at 500 every time, so Sequence A is an arithmetic progression.

Sequence B is not an AP. The consecutive differences are: 12500 − 10000 = 2500, 15625 − 12500 = 3125, 19531.25 − 15625 = 3906.25. The differences are not equal — they keep growing — because each term is multiplied by 5/4, not increased by a fixed addition. Therefore Sequence B is not an AP.
recall_questions.prompt: Look at these two sequences: (A) 8000, 8500, 9000, 9500 and (B) 10000, 12500, 15625, 19531.25. Which sequence is an AP and which is not? Explain how you decide.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: Year 1 = ₹ 100, Year 2 = ₹ 150, Year 3 = ₹ 200, Year 4 = ₹ 250.
Formula/Rule: A sequence is an AP if every consecutive difference aₖ₊₁ − aₖ is the same constant.
Substitution:
  a₂ − a₁ = 150 − 100 = 50
  a₃ − a₂ = 200 − 150 = 50
  a₄ − a₃ = 250 − 200 = 50
Calculation: All three differences equal 50.
Result: The friend is correct. The savings sequence 100, 150, 200, 250, … is an AP with first term a = 100 and common difference d = 50.
recall_questions.prompt: Priya saves ₹100 in year 1 and increases savings by ₹50 each year. A friend claims this forms an AP. Justify by computing consecutive differences for the first four years.

topics.topic_name: Defining an Arithmetic Progression — Common Difference, General Form, and Finite vs Infinite AP
topics.brief_summary: The common difference d = aₖ₊₁ − aₖ and the general form a, a + d, a + 2d, … are defined formally, and finite versus infinite APs are distinguished by whether a last term exists.
topics.modified_chunk:
RECALL: In the previous section, you examined six sequences and identified that some grew by a constant addition at every step while others followed different rules. We now formalise this observation into a precise definition.

5.2 Arithmetic Progressions

Consider the following lists of numbers:
(i) 1, 2, 3, 4, . . .
(ii) 100, 70, 40, 10, . . .
(iii) – 3, –2, –1, 0, . . .
(iv) 3, 3, 3, 3, . . .
(v) –1.0, –1.5, –2.0, –2.5, . . .

Each of the numbers in the list is called a term.

Given a term, can you write the next term in each of the lists above? If so, how will you write it? Perhaps by following a pattern or rule. Let us observe and write the rule.

In (i), each term is 1 more than the term preceding it.
In (ii), each term is 30 less than the term preceding it.
In (iii), each term is obtained by adding 1 to the term preceding it.
In (iv), all the terms in the list are 3, i.e., each term is obtained by adding (or subtracting) 0 to the term preceding it.
In (v), each term is obtained by adding – 0.5 to (i.e., subtracting 0.5 from) the term preceding it.

In all the lists above, we see that successive terms are obtained by adding a fixed number to the preceding terms. Such list of numbers is said to form an Arithmetic Progression ( AP ).

So, an arithmetic progression is a list of numbers in which each term is obtained by adding a fixed number to the preceding term except the first term.

This fixed number is called the common difference of the AP. Remember that it can be positive, negative or zero.

WHY THIS STEP? The common difference d is permitted to be negative (as in lists (ii) and (v)) or zero (as in list (iv), where all terms equal 3). Many students assume d must be a positive number; that assumption is incorrect. A sequence with d = 0 is a perfectly valid arithmetic progression in which all terms are equal.

Let us denote the first term of an AP by a₁, second term by a₂, . . ., nth term by aₙ and the common difference by d. Then the AP becomes a₁, a₂, a₃, . . ., aₙ.

So, a₂ – a₁ = a₃ – a₂ = . . . = aₙ – aₙ₋₁ = d.

This chain of equal differences is the defining test: if every consecutive difference equals the same value d, the sequence is an AP. If even one consecutive difference differs from the others, the sequence is not an AP.

Some more examples of AP are:

(a) The heights (in cm) of some students of a school standing in a queue in the morning assembly are 147, 148, 149, . . ., 157.

(b) The minimum temperatures (in degree celsius) recorded for a week in the month of January in a city, arranged in ascending order are

– 3.1, – 3.0, – 2.9, – 2.8, – 2.7, – 2.6, – 2.5

(c) The balance money (in ₹) after paying 5 % of the total loan of ₹ 1000 every month is 950, 900, 850, 800, . . ., 50.

(d) The cash prizes (in ₹) given by a school to the toppers of Classes I to XII are, respectively, 200, 250, 300, 350, . . ., 750.

(e) The total savings (in ₹) after every month for 10 months when ₹ 50 are saved each month are 50, 100, 150, 200, 250, 300, 350, 400, 450, 500.

It is left as an exercise for you to explain why each of the lists above is an AP.

You can see that

a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d, . . .

represents an arithmetic progression where a is the first term and d the common difference. This is called the general form of an AP.

Note that in examples (a) to (e) above, there are only a finite number of terms. Such an AP is called a finite AP. Also note that each of these Arithmetic Progressions (APs) has a last term. The APs in examples (i) to (v) in this section, are not finite APs and so they are called infinite Arithmetic Progressions. Such APs do not have a last term.

Now, to know about an AP, what is the minimum information that you need? Is it enough to know the first term? Or, is it enough to know only the common difference? You will find that you will need to know both – the first term a and the common difference d.

For instance if the first term a is 6 and the common difference d is 3, then the AP is

6, 9, 12, 15, . . .

and if a is 6 and d is – 3, then the AP is

6, 3, 0, –3, . . .

Similarly, when
a = – 7, d = – 2, the AP is – 7, – 9, – 11, – 13, . . .
a = 1.0, d = 0.1, the AP is 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, . . .
a = 0, d = 1½, the AP is 0, 1½, 3, 4½, 6, . . .
a = 2, d = 0, the AP is 2, 2, 2, 2, . . .

So, if you know what a and d are, you can list the AP. What about the other way round? That is, if you are given a list of numbers can you say that it is an AP and then find a and d? Since a is the first term, it can easily be written. We know that in an AP, every succeeding term is obtained by adding d to the preceding term. So, d found by subtracting any term from its succeeding term, i.e., the term which immediately follows it should be same for an AP.

For example, for the list of numbers:

6, 9, 12, 15, . . . ,

We have a₂ – a₁ = 9 – 6 = 3,
a₃ – a₂ = 12 – 9 = 3,
a₄ – a₃ = 15 – 12 = 3

Here the difference of any two consecutive terms in each case is 3. So, the given list is an AP whose first term a is 6 and common difference d is 3.

For the list of numbers: 6, 3, 0, – 3, . . .,
a₂ – a₁ = 3 – 6 = – 3
a₃ – a₂ = 0 – 3 = – 3
a₄ – a₃ = –3 – 0 = –3

Similarly this is also an AP whose first term is 6 and the common difference is –3.

In general, for an AP a₁, a₂, . . ., aₙ, we have

d = aₖ₊₁ – aₖ

where aₖ₊₁ and aₖ are the (k + 1)th and the kth terms respectively.

To obtain d in a given AP, we need not find all of a₂ – a₁, a₃ – a₂, a₄ – a₃, . . . . It is enough to find only one of them.

Consider the list of numbers 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, . . . . By looking at it, you can tell that the difference between any two consecutive terms is not the same. So, this is not an AP.

Note that to find d in the AP: 6, 3, 0, – 3, . . ., we have subtracted 6 from 3 and not 3 from 6, i.e., we should subtract the kth term from the (k + 1) th term even if the (k + 1) th term is smaller. Let us make the concept more clear through some examples.

ERROR ALERT: The direction of subtraction for d is fixed: always d = aₖ₊₁ − aₖ, meaning the later term minus the earlier term. If you reverse this — computing aₖ − aₖ₊₁ — you obtain the negative of d, which leads to systematic errors in every subsequent calculation. In the AP 6, 3, 0, –3, . . ., the correct common difference is d = 3 − 6 = −3, not +3. Always confirm the sign of d by computing at least two consecutive differences before using it in any formula.

CHECK: For each of the five lists (i)–(v) at the beginning of Section 5.2, write down the values of a and d, then verify by listing the next two terms using the rule aₖ₊₁ = aₖ + d.
topics.original_chunk:
5.2 Arithmetic Progressions

Consider the following lists of numbers:
(i) 1, 2, 3, 4, . . .
(ii) 100, 70, 40, 10, . . .
(iii) – 3, –2, –1, 0, . . .
(iv) 3, 3, 3, 3, . . .
(v) –1.0, –1.5, –2.0, –2.5, . . .

Each of the numbers in the list is called a term.

Given a term, can you write the next term in each of the lists above? If so, how will you write it? Perhaps by following a pattern or rule. Let us observe and write the rule.

In (i), each term is 1 more than the term preceding it.
In (ii), each term is 30 less than the term preceding it.
In (iii), each term is obtained by adding 1 to the term preceding it.
In (iv), all the terms in the list are 3, i.e., each term is obtained by adding (or subtracting) 0 to the term preceding it.
In (v), each term is obtained by adding – 0.5 to (i.e., subtracting 0.5 from) the term preceding it.

In all the lists above, we see that successive terms are obtained by adding a fixed number to the preceding terms. Such list of numbers is said to form an Arithmetic Progression ( AP ).

So, an arithmetic progression is a list of numbers in which each term is obtained by adding a fixed number to the preceding term except the first term.

This fixed number is called the common difference of the AP. Remember that it can be positive, negative or zero.

Let us denote the first term of an AP by a₁, second term by a₂, . . ., nth term by aₙ and the common difference by d. Then the AP becomes a₁, a₂, a₃, . . ., aₙ.

So, a₂ – a₁ = a₃ – a₂ = . . . = aₙ – aₙ₋₁ = d.

Some more examples of AP are:

(a) The heights (in cm) of some students of a school standing in a queue in the morning assembly are 147, 148, 149, . . ., 157.

(b) The minimum temperatures (in degree celsius) recorded for a week in the month of January in a city, arranged in ascending order are

– 3.1, – 3.0, – 2.9, – 2.8, – 2.7, – 2.6, – 2.5

(c) The balance money (in ₹) after paying 5 % of the total loan of ₹ 1000 every month is 950, 900, 850, 800, . . ., 50.

(d) The cash prizes (in ₹) given by a school to the toppers of Classes I to XII are, respectively, 200, 250, 300, 350, . . ., 750.

(e) The total savings (in ₹) after every month for 10 months when ₹ 50 are saved each month are 50, 100, 150, 200, 250, 300, 350, 400, 450, 500.

It is left as an exercise for you to explain why each of the lists above is an AP.

You can see that

a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d, . . .

represents an arithmetic progression where a is the first term and d the common difference. This is called the general form of an AP.

Note that in examples (a) to (e) above, there are only a finite number of terms. Such an AP is called a finite AP. Also note that each of these Arithmetic Progressions (APs) has a last term. The APs in examples (i) to (v) in this section, are not finite APs and so they are called infinite Arithmetic Progressions. Such APs do not have a last term.

Now, to know about an AP, what is the minimum information that you need? Is it enough to know the first term? Or, is it enough to know only the common difference? You will find that you will need to know both – the first term a and the common difference d.

For instance if the first term a is 6 and the common difference d is 3, then the AP is

6, 9, 12, 15, . . .

and if a is 6 and d is – 3, then the AP is

6, 3, 0, –3, . . .

Similarly, when
a = – 7, d = – 2, the AP is – 7, – 9, – 11, – 13, . . .
a = 1.0, d = 0.1, the AP is 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, . . .
a = 0, d = 1½, the AP is 0, 1½, 3, 4½, 6, . . .
a = 2, d = 0, the AP is 2, 2, 2, 2, . . .

So, if you know what a and d are, you can list the AP. What about the other way round? That is, if you are given a list of numbers can you say that it is an AP and then find a and d? Since a is the first term, it can easily be written. We know that in an AP, every succeeding term is obtained by adding d to the preceding term. So, d found by subtracting any term from its succeeding term, i.e., the term which immediately follows it should be same for an AP.

For example, for the list of numbers:

6, 9, 12, 15, . . . ,

We have a₂ – a₁ = 9 – 6 = 3,
a₃ – a₂ = 12 – 9 = 3,
a₄ – a₃ = 15 – 12 = 3

Here the difference of any two consecutive terms in each case is 3. So, the given list is an AP whose first term a is 6 and common difference d is 3.

For the list of numbers: 6, 3, 0, – 3, . . .,
a₂ – a₁ = 3 – 6 = – 3
a₃ – a₂ = 0 – 3 = – 3
a₄ – a₃ = –3 – 0 = –3

Similarly this is also an AP whose first term is 6 and the common difference is –3.

In general, for an AP a₁, a₂, . . ., aₙ, we have

d = aₖ₊₁ – aₖ

where aₖ₊₁ and aₖ are the (k + 1)th and the kth terms respectively.

To obtain d in a given AP, we need not find all of a₂ – a₁, a₃ – a₂, a₄ – a₃, . . . . It is enough to find only one of them.

Consider the list of numbers 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, . . . . By looking at it, you can tell that the difference between any two consecutive terms is not the same. So, this is not an AP.

Note that to find d in the AP: 6, 3, 0, – 3, . . ., we have subtracted 6 from 3 and not 3 from 6, i.e., we should subtract the kth term from the (k + 1) th term even if the (k + 1) th term is smaller. Let us make the concept more clear through some examples.
concept_bullets: d = aₖ₊₁ − aₖ is always computed as the later term minus the earlier term — for example, in 6, 3, 0, −3, … we get d = 3 − 6 = −3, not +3.
d can be positive, negative, or zero — for example, the AP 2, 2, 2, 2, … has d = 0 and is a valid AP where all terms are equal.
A finite AP has a last term — for example, 950, 900, 850, …, 50 ends at 50 — while an infinite AP such as 1, 2, 3, 4, … continues without end.
Knowing both a and d completely determines the AP — for example, a = 6 and d = 3 gives 6, 9, 12, 15, …, while a = 6 and d = −3 gives 6, 3, 0, −3, …

recall_questions.answer: An arithmetic progression (AP) is a list of numbers in which each term is obtained by adding a fixed number to the preceding term (except the first term). This fixed number is called the common difference d. Using notation: for an AP a₁, a₂, a₃, …, aₙ, the common difference is d = aₖ₊₁ − aₖ for any consecutive pair, where the later term is always subtracted from first (later minus earlier).
recall_questions.prompt: State the definition of an arithmetic progression and define the common difference d using proper notation.

recall_questions.answer: The student is incorrect. The sequence 3, 3, 3, 3 is a perfectly valid AP. The common difference is d = 3 − 3 = 0. The definition of an AP allows d to be zero — it simply means all terms are equal. The common difference can be positive, negative, or zero. A constant sequence satisfies the condition that every consecutive difference is the same (equal to zero), so it qualifies as an AP.
recall_questions.prompt: A student says 3, 3, 3, 3 is not an AP because nothing changes. Is the student correct? Explain and state the value of d.

recall_questions.answer:
Error: The student subtracted the earlier term from the later term in the wrong order. The correct formula is d = aₖ₊₁ − aₖ (later term minus earlier term), not aₖ − aₖ₊₁.

Correct working:
  d = a₂ − a₁ = 3 − 6 = −3
  Verification: a₃ − a₂ = 0 − 3 = −3 ✓ and a₄ − a₃ = −3 − 0 = −3 ✓

The correct common difference is d = −3. The AP is decreasing, and d must be negative to reflect that each term is 3 less than the previous one.
recall_questions.prompt: For the AP 6, 3, 0, −3, a student wrote d = 6 − 3 = 3. Identify the error and state the correct value of d.

recall_questions.answer:
Sequence (i) Reena's salary: 8000, 8500, 9000. Differences: 500, 500. Constant → AP (d = 500).
Sequence (ii) Ladder rungs: 45, 43, 41. Differences: −2, −2. Constant → AP (d = −2).
Sequence (iii) Savings scheme: 10000, 12500, 15625. Differences: 2500, 3125. Not constant (multiplied by 5/4) → Not AP.
Sequence (iv) Unit squares: 1, 4, 9, 16. Differences: 3, 5, 7. Not constant (odd numbers, growing) → Not AP.
Sequence (v) Shakila's savings: 100, 150, 200. Differences: 50, 50. Constant → AP (d = 50).
Sequence (vi) Rabbit pairs: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5. Differences: 0, 1, 1. Not constant (Fibonacci pattern) → Not AP.

Summary: Sequences (i), (ii), and (v) are APs; sequences (iii), (iv), and (vi) are not APs.
recall_questions.prompt: From the six sequences in Section 5.1, two are APs and four are not. Using the definition of common difference from Section 5.2, classify all six sequences as AP or Not AP, computing at least two consecutive differences for each.

recall_questions.answer: The first term a fixes the starting point of the sequence. The common difference d fixes the rule by which every subsequent term is generated: each term equals the previous one plus d. Together, a and d uniquely determine every term of the AP — given any position n, the term is a + (n − 1)d — so no additional information is needed. Knowing only a would allow infinitely many APs (one for each possible value of d); knowing only d would leave the starting position undefined.
recall_questions.prompt: Explain in two or three sentences why knowing both the first term a and the common difference d is necessary and sufficient to fully describe an arithmetic progression.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: Sequence 200, 250, 300, …, 750.
Step 1 — Verify AP (AP definition from T1/T2): Compute consecutive differences.
  250 − 200 = 50, 300 − 250 = 50. Differences are equal → AP confirmed.
  d = 50.
Step 2 — General form (T2 concept: a, a + d, a + 2d, …):
  a = 200, d = 50.
  General form: 200, 250, 300, 350, …, 750.
  Or in algebraic notation: aₙ = 200 + (n − 1) × 50.
Verification of last term: aₙ = 750 → 200 + (n − 1) × 50 = 750 → (n − 1) × 50 = 550 → n − 1 = 11 → n = 12. So there are 12 terms (Classes I to XII) ✓.

topics.modified_chunk:
RECALL: A list of numbers forms an AP if every consecutive difference aₖ₊₁ − aₖ equals the same constant d. If even one consecutive difference differs from the others, the sequence is not an AP. The following two examples practise reading a and d from a given AP, and testing whether a given list qualifies.

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — Complete:

Example 1: For the AP : 3/2, 1/2, – 1/2, – 3/2 , . . ., write the first term a and the common difference d.

Solution: Here, a = 3/2, d = 1/2 – 3/2 = – 1.

WHY THIS STEP? We compute d = a₂ − a₁ = 1/2 − 3/2 = −1. The direction is always later term minus earlier term, never the reverse. Quick verification: 3/2 + (−1) = 1/2 ✓, and 1/2 + (−1) = −1/2 ✓, confirming d = −1 throughout.

Remember that we can find d using any two consecutive terms, once we know that the numbers are in AP.

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — Partially faded (work through cases (i) and (ii) in full; verify cases (iii) and (iv) yourself by computing the first two consecutive differences before reading ahead):

Example 2: Which of the following list of numbers form an AP? If they form an AP, write the next two terms:
(i) 4, 10, 16, 22, . . . (ii) 1, – 1, – 3, – 5, . . .
(iii) – 2, 2, – 2, 2, – 2, . . . (iv) 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, . . .

Solution: (i) We have a₂ – a₁ = 10 – 4 = 6
a₃ – a₂ = 16 – 10 = 6
a₄ – a₃ = 22 – 16 = 6

i.e., aₖ₊₁ – aₖ is the same every time.
So, the given list of numbers forms an AP with the common difference d = 6.
The next two terms are: 22 + 6 = 28 and 28 + 6 = 34.

(ii) a₂ – a₁ = – 1 – 1 = – 2
a₃ – a₂ = – 3 – ( –1 ) = – 3 + 1 = – 2
a₄ – a₃ = – 5 – ( –3 ) = – 5 + 3 = – 2

i.e., aₖ₊₁ – aₖ is the same every time.
So, the given list of numbers forms an AP with the common difference d = – 2.
The next two terms are:
– 5 + (– 2) = – 7 and – 7 + (– 2) = – 9

(iii) a₂ – a₁ = 2 – (– 2) = 2 + 2 = 4
a₃ – a₂ = – 2 – 2 = – 4

As a₂ – a₁ ≠ a₃ – a₂, the given list of numbers does not form an AP.

(iv) a₂ – a₁ = 1 – 1 = 0
a₃ – a₂ = 1 – 1 = 0
a₄ – a₃ = 2 – 1 = 1

Here, a₂ – a₁ = a₃ – a₂ ≠ a₄ – a₃.
So, the given list of numbers does not form an AP.

ERROR ALERT: Do not conclude from just two equal consecutive differences that a sequence is an AP. In case (iv), the first two differences both equal zero, which might suggest d = 0. The third difference immediately contradicts this. The AP test requires every consecutive difference — across the entire sequence — to be equal, not merely the first few.

CHECK: For the AP in case (i), confirm d = 6 by computing a₅ − a₄ and a₆ − a₅ using the terms 28 and 34 you just found.

Example 1 : For the AP : 3/2, 1/2, – 1/2, – 3/2 , . . ., write the first term a and the common difference d.

Solution : Here, a = 3/2, d = 1/2 – 3/2 = – 1.

Remember that we can find d using any two consecutive terms, once we know that the numbers are in AP.

Example 2 : Which of the following list of numbers form an AP? If they form an AP, write the next two terms:
(i) 4, 10, 16, 22, . . . (ii) 1, – 1, – 3, – 5, . . .
(iii) – 2, 2, – 2, 2, – 2, . . . (iv) 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, . . .

a₃ – a₂ = 16 – 10 = 6
a₄ – a₃ = 22 – 16 = 6

i.e., aₖ₊₁ – aₖ is the same every time.
So, the given list of numbers forms an AP with the common difference d = 6.
The next two terms are: 22 + 6 = 28 and 28 + 6 = 34.

(ii) a₂ – a₁ = – 1 – 1 = – 2
a₃ – a₂ = – 3 – ( –1 ) = – 3 + 1 = – 2
a₄ – a₃ = – 5 – ( –3 ) = – 5 + 3 = – 2

i.e., aₖ₊₁ – aₖ is the same every time.
So, the given list of numbers forms an AP with the common difference d = – 2.
The next two terms are:
– 5 + (– 2) = – 7 and – 7 + (– 2) = – 9

(iii) a₂ – a₁ = 2 – (– 2) = 2 + 2 = 4
a₃ – a₂ = – 2 – 2 = – 4

As a₂ – a₁ ≠ a₃ – a₂, the given list of numbers does not form an AP.

(iv) a₂ – a₁ = 1 – 1 = 0
a₃ – a₂ = 1 – 1 = 0
a₄ – a₃ = 2 – 1 = 1

Here, a₂ – a₁ = a₃ – a₂ ≠ a₄ – a₃.

concept_bullets: Every consecutive difference must be equal for a sequence to be an AP — for example, 4, 10, 16, 22 has differences 6, 6, 6 so d = 6 ✓, while −2, 2, −2, 2 has differences +4, −4 so it is not an AP.
A single unequal difference disqualifies the entire sequence — for example, 1, 1, 1, 2 has first two differences equal to 0 but the third difference is 1, so it fails the test.
d is found by computing aₖ₊₁ − aₖ for any one consecutive pair once the sequence is confirmed as an AP — for example, in 1, −1, −3, −5 we use d = −1 − 1 = −2.
The next two terms of an AP are found by adding d twice — for example, after 22 in the AP with d = 6, the next terms are 22 + 6 = 28 and 28 + 6 = 34.

recall_questions.answer:
Step 1: Compute the difference a₂ − a₁ (second term minus first term).
Step 2: Compute a₃ − a₂, a₄ − a₃, and so on for all consecutive pairs.
Step 3: If every consecutive difference equals the same value d, the list is an AP with common difference d.
Step 4: If even one consecutive difference differs from the others, the list is not an AP.
Note: It is not sufficient to check just the first two differences; the test must be applied across the entire sequence.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: Sequence 4, 10, 16, 22.
Formula/Rule: Compute all consecutive differences aₖ₊₁ − aₖ.
Substitution:
  a₂ − a₁ = 10 − 4 = 6
  a₃ − a₂ = 16 − 10 = 6
  a₄ − a₃ = 22 − 16 = 6
Calculation: All consecutive differences equal 6.
Result: The list is an AP with a = 4 and d = 6.
Next two terms: 22 + 6 = 28, and 28 + 6 = 34.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: Sequence 3/2, 1/2, −1/2, −3/2, …
Formula/Rule: a = first term; d = a₂ − a₁.
Substitution:
  a = 3/2
  d = 1/2 − 3/2 = (1 − 3)/2 = −2/2 = −1
Verification: −1/2 − 1/2 = −1 ✓ and −3/2 − (−1/2) = −3/2 + 1/2 = −1 ✓
Next two terms:
  5th term = −3/2 + (−1) = −3/2 − 2/2 = −5/2
  6th term = −5/2 + (−1) = −7/2
Result: a = 3/2, d = −1, and the next two terms are −5/2 and −7/2.

topics.summary: Exercise 5.1 practises three AP skills across 15 questions: classifying real-world and abstract sequences as APs by reasoning about whether the generating process adds a constant, writing the first four terms of an AP when a and d are given, and identifying a and d from a given sequence.
topics.topic_name: Exercise 5.1 — Classifying Sequences and Writing AP Terms
topics.brief_summary: Exercise 5.1 consolidates AP classification and term-generation skills by applying the constant-difference criterion to real-world situations and abstract lists across 15 practice questions.
topics.modified_chunk:
This exercise consolidates your ability to recognise arithmetic progressions across a range of real-world and abstract situations, to determine the first term a and common difference d from a given sequence, and to extend or construct sequences using the AP rule. For Question 1, reason carefully about the physical process generating each sequence — the key question is whether the additive change between successive terms is constant. For Question 4, compute at least two consecutive differences before drawing a conclusion.

EXERCISE 5.1

1. In which of the following situations, does the list of numbers involved make an arithmetic progression, and why?
(i) The taxi fare after each km when the fare is ₹ 15 for the first km and ₹ 8 for each additional km.
(ii) The amount of air present in a cylinder when a vacuum pump removes 1/4 of the air remaining in the cylinder at a time.
(iii) The cost of digging a well after every metre of digging, when it costs ₹ 150 for the first metre and rises by ₹ 50 for each subsequent metre.
(iv) The amount of money in the account every year, when ₹ 10000 is deposited at compound interest at 8 % per annum.

2. Write first four terms of the AP, when the first term a and the common difference d are given as follows:
(i) a = 10, d = 10 (ii) a = –2, d = 0
(iii) a = 4, d = – 3 (iv) a = – 1, d = 1/2
(v) a = – 1.25, d = – 0.25

3. For the following APs, write the first term and the common difference:
(i) 3, 1, – 1, – 3, . . . (ii) – 5, – 1, 3, 7, . . .
(iii) 1/3, 5/3, 9/3, 13/3, . . . (iv) 0.6, 1.7, 2.8, 3.9, . . .

4. Which of the following are APs ? If they form an AP, find the common difference d and write three more terms.
(i) 2, 4, 8, 16, . . . (ii) 2, 5/2, 3, 7/2, . . .
(iii) – 1.2, – 3.2, – 5.2, – 7.2, . . . (iv) – 10, – 6, – 2, 2, . . .
(v) 3, 3 + √2, 3 + 2√2, 3 + 3√2, . . . (vi) 0.2, 0.22, 0.222, 0.2222, . . .
(vii) 0, – 4, – 8, –12, . . . (viii) – 1/2, – 1/2, – 1/2, – 1/2, . . .
(ix) 1, 3, 9, 27, . . . (x) a, 2a, 3a, 4a, . . .
(xi) a, a², a³, a⁴, . . . (xii) √2, √8, √18, √32, . . .
(xiii) √3, √6, √9, √12, . . . (xiv) 1², 3², 5², 7², . . .
(xv) 1², 5², 7², 73, . . .

Note: For Question 1(ii) and 1(iv), recall that removing a fraction of a remaining quantity and applying compound interest both involve multiplication at each step — this changes the amount by a varying quantity, not a fixed one. Use this reasoning to justify your answers.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: First km costs ₹ 15; each additional km costs ₹ 8.
Formula/Rule: Total fare after km 1 = 15; after km 2 = 15 + 8 = 23; after km n = 15 + (n − 1) × 8.
Substitution:
  km 1: ₹ 15
  km 2: ₹ 23
  km 3: ₹ 31
  km 4: ₹ 39
  km 5: ₹ 47
Calculation of differences: 23 − 15 = 8, 31 − 23 = 8, 39 − 31 = 8, 47 − 39 = 8. All equal.
Result: The sequence 15, 23, 31, 39, 47, … is an AP with first term a = 15 and common difference d = 8.
recall_questions.prompt: The taxi fare in a city is ₹ 15 for the first kilometre and ₹ 8 for each additional kilometre. Write the first five terms of the fare sequence and determine whether it forms an AP. If yes, state a and d.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: a = 4, d = −3.
Formula/Rule: Each term = previous term + d = previous term + (−3).
Terms:
  a₁ = 4
  a₂ = 4 + (−3) = 1
  a₃ = 1 + (−3) = −2
  a₄ = −2 + (−3) = −5
Sequence: 4, 1, −2, −5.

Explanation: The definition of an AP requires that every consecutive difference aₖ₊₁ − aₖ is the same constant. Here, that constant is −3. The definition allows d to be negative, zero, or positive. A negative d simply means the sequence is decreasing. The key requirement — constant consecutive difference — is still satisfied, so it is a valid AP.
recall_questions.prompt: Write the first four terms of an AP with a = 4 and d = −3. Then explain why the sequence is still called an AP even though the terms are decreasing.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: Sequence 1, 9, 25, 49 (squares of 1, 3, 5, 7).
Formula/Rule: Compute all consecutive differences to test the AP condition.
Substitution:
  a₂ − a₁ = 9 − 1 = 8
  a₃ − a₂ = 25 − 9 = 16
  a₄ − a₃ = 49 − 25 = 24
Calculation: The differences are 8, 16, 24 — they are not equal.
Result: The student's claim is incorrect. Even though the terms follow a pattern (squares of odd numbers), the consecutive differences are not constant. Therefore, 1, 9, 25, 49 is NOT an AP. Following a pattern does not automatically make a sequence an AP — the pattern must specifically be adding a constant difference at every step.

  6th term = 5√2 + √2 = 6√2 = √72.

recall_questions.prompt: From Exercise 5.1 Q4, the sequence √2, √8, √18, √32 was identified as an AP. Verify this claim by computing consecutive differences in simplified form, and then write the next two terms.

recall_questions.answer:
Sequence A: 2, 5/2, 3, 7/2.
  Differences: 5/2 − 2 = 1/2; 3 − 5/2 = 1/2; 7/2 − 3 = 1/2. All equal 1/2 → AP with d = 1/2.

Sequence B: 0.2, 0.22, 0.222, 0.2222.
  Differences: 0.22 − 0.20 = 0.02; 0.222 − 0.22 = 0.002; 0.2222 − 0.222 = 0.0002. Differences 0.02, 0.002, 0.0002 are not equal → Not AP.

Mistake: The student likely judged by visual inspection alone — perhaps assuming fractional or non-round terms cannot form an AP, or that terms with increasing decimal digits must be an AP. The correct method is always to compute all consecutive differences numerically. Sequence A looks like it has fractions but has a perfectly constant difference; Sequence B looks like it has a pattern but the differences keep shrinking by a factor of 10.
recall_questions.prompt: A student tested two sequences: (A) 2, 5/2, 3, 7/2 and (B) 0.2, 0.22, 0.222, 0.2222. She incorrectly labelled both as 'Not AP' after a quick visual check. Show, by computing differences, which is actually an AP and which is not. Explain what mistake the student likely made.

recall_questions.answer:
Taxi fare (AP): Fare for km 1 = ₹ 15; km 2 = ₹ 23; km 3 = ₹ 31.
  Differences: 23 − 15 = 8; 31 − 23 = 8. Constant d = 8. The fare increases by the same fixed amount (₹ 8) for every additional km — this is additive growth, which is the defining property of an AP.

Compound interest (Not AP): Each year the interest is calculated on the new, larger balance. So the amount added each year grows bigger every year. For ₹ 10000 at 8%: Year 1 adds ₹ 800, Year 2 adds ₹ 864, Year 3 adds ₹ 933.12 — differences are not constant.

Conclusion: Constant additive growth → AP. Multiplicative (percentage of growing base) growth → not an AP. The key test is always whether consecutive differences are equal.
recall_questions.prompt: In Exercise 5.1, the taxi fare sequence (₹ 15, ₹ 23, ₹ 31, …) and the compound interest sequence both grow over time. Using the methods from this segment, explain why one is an AP and the other is not, and state what type of growth each represents.

modules.module_name: Foundations — Understanding and Recognising Arithmetic Progressions
modules.brief_summary: Module 1 develops the ability to recognise and define arithmetic progressions, distinguishing AP sequences from non-AP sequences using the constant-difference test across Segments M1.S1 and M1.S2.
modules.detailed_summary: Module 1 builds the foundational ability to recognise, define, and verify arithmetic progressions from both real-world contexts and lists of numbers. Segment M1.S1 establishes the formal definition of an AP — including the common difference d and the general form a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d, … — by first examining everyday sequences such as salary increments and savings deposits. Segment M1.S2 develops the skill of testing whether any given list is an AP by checking whether aₖ₊₁ − aₖ is constant across all consecutive pairs, and extends this to classifying real-world situations and writing AP terms when a and d are given. The unifying mathematical insight is that an AP is completely determined by just two numbers — its first term a and its common difference d — and that every subsequent term is generated by a single, repeating additive step. This two-parameter structure underpins all subsequent work with the nth term formula and the sum formula in later modules.
important_points: an arithmetic progression is a list of numbers in which each term is obtained by adding a fixed number to the preceding term except the first term.
This fixed number is called the common difference of the AP. Remember that it can be positive, negative or zero.

a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d, . . .

represents an arithmetic progression where a is the first term and d the common difference. This is called the general form of an AP.
In all the lists above, we see that successive terms are obtained by adding a fixed number to the preceding terms. Such list of numbers is said to form an Arithmetic Progression ( AP ).

d = aₖ₊₁ – aₖ

where aₖ₊₁ and aₖ are the (k + 1)th and the kth terms respectively.
Note that in examples (a) to (e) above, there are only a finite number of terms. Such an AP is called a finite AP.
The APs in examples (i) to (v) in this section, are not finite APs and so they are called infinite Arithmetic Progressions. Such APs do not have a last term.
Remember that we can find d using any two consecutive terms, once we know that the numbers are in AP.
As a₂ – a₁ ≠ a₃ – a₂, the given list of numbers does not form an AP.

modules.summary: Module 2 derives and applies the nth term formula aₙ = a + (n − 1)d, enabling students to compute any term of an AP directly without iterating through all preceding terms. Segment M2.S3 first builds the formula from the pattern of repeated addition seen in Reena's salary sequence, then applies it in four distinct modes — forward computation, inverse position-finding, reconstruction from two known terms, and AP membership testing. The key algebraic insight that drives the module is the off-by-one structure: the coefficient of d is always (n − 1) because the first term requires zero additions. Once students master this, they can answer questions about APs of any length in a single substitution step, setting the stage for the sum formula in Module 3.

topics.topic_name: From Pattern to Formula — Deriving aₙ = a + (n − 1)d
topics.brief_summary: The nth term formula aₙ = a + (n − 1)d is derived from the salary-increment pattern, where the coefficient (n − 1) counts the additions of d needed to reach the nth position from the first term.
topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: You now know that Reena's salary forms an arithmetic progression: ₹ 8000, ₹ 8500, ₹ 9000, . . ., with a = 8000 and d = 500. Computing her salary for year 5 requires four additions of 500. But what if you needed her salary for year 25 or year 50? Repeating the addition 24 or 49 times is tedious and error-prone. This section derives a single formula that gives the nth term of any AP immediately, using only a, d, and n.

RECALL: An AP is fully determined by its first term a and common difference d. The general form is a, a + d, a + 2d, a + 3d, . . . . Each term is the previous term plus d. What we now seek is a direct expression for the nth term aₙ in terms of a, d, and n — without computing all intermediate terms.

5.3 nth Term of an AP

Let us consider the situation again, given in Section 5.1 in which Reena applied for a job and got selected. She has been offered the job with a starting monthly salary of ₹ 8000, with an annual increment of ₹ 500. What would be her monthly salary for the fifth year?

To answer this, let us first see what her monthly salary for the second year would be.

It would be ₹ (8000 + 500) = ₹ 8500. In the same way, we can find the monthly salary for the 3rd, 4th and 5th year by adding ₹ 500 to the salary of the previous year.

So, the salary for the 3rd year = ₹ (8500 + 500)
= ₹ (8000 + 500 + 500)
= ₹ (8000 + 2 × 500)
= ₹ [8000 + (3 – 1) × 500]  (for the 3rd year)
= ₹ 9000

Salary for the 4th year = ₹ (9000 + 500)
= ₹ (8000 + 500 + 500 + 500)
= ₹ (8000 + 3 × 500)
= ₹ [8000 + (4 – 1) × 500]  (for the 4th year)
= ₹ 9500

Salary for the 5th year = ₹ (9500 + 500)
= ₹ (8000+500+500+500 + 500)
= ₹ (8000 + 4 × 500)
= ₹ [8000 + (5 – 1) × 500]  (for the 5th year)
= ₹ 10000

WHY THIS STEP? Notice the pattern forming: the salary for year n is always ₹ [8000 + (n − 1) × 500]. The coefficient of 500 is always one less than the year number, because the first year requires zero additions, the second year requires one addition, and so on.

Observe that we are getting a list of numbers

8000, 8500, 9000, 9500, 10000, . . .

These numbers are in AP. (Why?)

Now, looking at the pattern formed above, can you find her monthly salary for the 6th year? The 15th year? And, assuming that she will still be working in the job, what about the monthly salary for the 25th year? You would calculate this by adding ₹ 500 each time to the salary of the previous year to give the answer. Can we make this process shorter? Let us see. You may have already got some idea from the way we have obtained the salaries above.

Salary for the 15th year
= Salary for the 14th year + ₹ 500
= ₹ [8000 + 14 × 500]
= ₹ [8000 + (15 – 1) × 500] = ₹ 15000
i.e., First salary + (15 – 1) × Annual increment.

In the same way, her monthly salary for the 25th year would be
₹ [8000 + (25 – 1) × 500] = ₹ 20000
= First salary + (25 – 1) × Annual increment

This example would have given you some idea about how to write the 15th term, or the 25th term, and more generally, the nth term of the AP.

Let a₁, a₂, a₃, . . . be an AP whose first term a₁ is a and the common difference is d.

Then,
the second term a₂ = a + d = a + (2 – 1) d
the third term a₃ = a₂ + d = (a + d) + d = a + 2d = a + (3 – 1) d
the fourth term a₄ = a₃ + d = (a + 2d) + d = a + 3d = a + (4 – 1) d
. . . . . . . .
. . . . . . . .

Looking at the pattern, we can say that the nth term aₙ = a + (n – 1) d.

So, the nth term aₙ of the AP with first term a and common difference d is given by

aₙ = a + (n – 1) d

aₙ is also called the general term of the AP. If there are m terms in the AP, then aₘ represents the last term which is sometimes also denoted by l.

EX1 CALLBACK: This formula applies directly to Priya's monthly savings introduced at the start of this chapter. With a = 200 and d = 50, her savings in month n are aₙ = 200 + (n − 1) × 50. In month 12, she saves ₹ [200 + 11 × 50] = ₹ [200 + 550] = ₹ 750. The formula replaces eleven successive additions with a single computation.

ERROR ALERT: The most frequent error with this formula is writing aₙ = a + nd instead of aₙ = a + (n − 1)d. To understand why the subtraction of 1 is necessary: the first term (n = 1) requires zero additions of d, so the multiplier is n − 1 = 0, giving a₁ = a + 0 = a. Using nd instead gives a₁ = a + d, which is wrong by exactly one step. When n = 1, always verify that your formula returns a₁ = a before proceeding.

CHECK: Using aₙ = a + (n − 1)d, confirm that Reena's salary for the 25th year is ₹ 20000 as stated above. Then substitute n = 1 into the formula to verify that it correctly returns ₹ 8000.

Let us consider some examples.

recall_questions.answer: The nth term of an AP is given by: aₙ = a + (n − 1)d, where a is the first term of the AP, d is the common difference, n is the position of the term (a positive integer), and aₙ is the value of the nth term. The term aₙ is also called the general term of the AP.
recall_questions.prompt: State the formula for the nth term of an arithmetic progression, naming each variable in the formula.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: a = 8000 (starting salary), d = 500 (annual increment), n = 25.
Formula/Rule: aₙ = a + (n − 1)d.
Substitution: a₂₅ = 8000 + (25 − 1) × 500.
Calculation: a₂₅ = 8000 + 24 × 500 = 8000 + 12000 = 20000.
Result: Reena's monthly salary in the 25th year is ₹ 20,000.
recall_questions.prompt: Reena's starting monthly salary is ₹ 8000 with an annual increment of ₹ 500. Using the formula aₙ = a + (n − 1)d, find her salary in the 25th year. Show each step clearly.

recall_questions.answer:
Error: The student used aₙ = a + nd instead of the correct formula aₙ = a + (n − 1)d. This is an off-by-one error — it overcounts the number of times d is added.

Why it occurs: The first term a₁ is obtained with zero additions of d (since n = 1 gives n − 1 = 0). Using nd gives the first term as a + d, which is actually the second term. Every subsequent term is therefore off by one step.

Correct working:
  Given: a = 5, d = 3, n = 10.
  a₁₀ = 5 + (10 − 1) × 3 = 5 + 9 × 3 = 5 + 27 = 32.

Verification: When n = 1, a₁ = 5 + (1 − 1) × 3 = 5 + 0 = 5 ✓.
Result: The correct value of a₁₀ is 32, not 35.

topics.summary: The formula aₙ = a + (n − 1)d is applied in four modes — forward (find aₙ given n), inverse (find n given aₙ), reconstruction (find a and d from two term conditions by solving simultaneous equations), and membership testing (check whether a target value is a term by verifying that the resulting n is a positive integer).
topics.topic_name: Applying the nth Term Formula — Finding Terms, Checking Membership, and Constructing APs
topics.brief_summary: Four distinct uses of aₙ = a + (n − 1)d are demonstrated: computing a₁₀ = 47 for AP 2, 7, 12, …; locating the 35th term equal to −81; reconstructing the AP 3, 4, 5, … from its 3rd and 7th terms; and proving 301 is not a term of 5, 11, 17, … because n = 151/3 is not an integer.
topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: The formula aₙ = a + (n − 1)d can be used in four distinct ways: finding a term given its position (forward), finding the position of a given term (inverse), reconstructing an AP from two term conditions (system of equations), and verifying whether a number belongs to a given AP at all (membership test). The following four examples develop each of these skills in turn.

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — Complete (forward application: find aₙ given n):

Example 3: Find the 10th term of the AP : 2, 7, 12, . . .

Solution: Here, a = 2, d = 7 – 2 = 5 and n = 10.
We have aₙ = a + (n – 1) d
So, a₁₀ = 2 + (10 – 1) × 5 = 2 + 45 = 47
Therefore, the 10th term of the given AP is 47.

WHY THIS STEP? We first identify the three knowns (a, d, n) and substitute directly. The calculation (10 − 1) × 5 = 9 × 5 = 45 counts the nine steps of size 5 taken from the first term to reach the tenth.

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — Complete (inverse application: find n given aₙ, and existence check):

Example 4: Which term of the AP : 21, 18, 15, . . . is – 81? Also, is any term 0? Give reason for your answer.

Solution: Here, a = 21, d = 18 – 21 = – 3 and aₙ = – 81, and we have to find n.

As aₙ = a + ( n – 1) d,
we have – 81 = 21 + (n – 1)(– 3)
– 81 = 24 – 3n
– 105 = – 3n
So, n = 35
Therefore, the 35th term of the given AP is – 81.

Next, we want to know if there is any n for which aₙ = 0. If such an n is there, then
21 + (n – 1) (–3) = 0,
i.e., 3(n – 1) = 21
i.e., n = 8
So, the eighth term is 0.

WHY THIS STEP? In the first part, we rearranged aₙ = a + (n − 1)d to solve for n. In the second part, we treated aₙ = 0 as a target value and solved the same equation for n, obtaining n = 8. Since 8 is a positive integer, a zero term does exist in this AP.

WORKED EXAMPLE 3 — Partially faded (write the two equations yourself before reading the solution):

Example 5: Determine the AP whose 3rd term is 5 and the 7th term is 9.

Solution: We have
a₃ = a + (3 – 1) d = a + 2d = 5   (1)
and a₇ = a + (7 – 1) d = a + 6d = 9   (2)
Solving the pair of linear equations (1) and (2), we get
a = 3, d = 1
Hence, the required AP is 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, . . .

WORKED EXAMPLE 4 — Further faded (set up the equation and evaluate whether n is valid):

Example 6: Check whether 301 is a term of the list of numbers 5, 11, 17, 23, . . .

Solution: We have:
a₂ – a₁ = 11 – 5 = 6,   a₃ – a₂ = 17 – 11 = 6,   a₄ – a₃ = 23 – 17 = 6

As aₖ₊₁ – aₖ is the same for k = 1, 2, 3, etc., the given list of numbers is an AP.
Now, a = 5 and d = 6.
Let 301 be a term, say, the nth term of this AP.
We know that
aₙ = a + (n – 1) d
So, 301 = 5 + (n – 1) × 6
i.e., 301 = 6n – 1
So, n = 302/6 = 151/3

But n should be a positive integer (Why?). So, 301 is not a term of the given list of numbers.

ERROR ALERT: The result n = 151/3 is not a positive integer. This is the decisive test for AP membership: the term number n must be a natural number (1, 2, 3, . . .). If solving aₙ = a + (n − 1)d for a given target value yields a non-integer or a negative result, the target value is NOT a term of the AP. The reason n must be a positive integer is that terms are indexed by position — there is no 151/3-th position in a list.

CHECK: For Example 5, verify that a = 3 and d = 1 satisfy BOTH equations (1) and (2) before accepting the answer. Then write the AP and confirm that the 3rd and 7th terms are indeed 5 and 9.

concept_bullets: Forward application: substitute a, d, and n into aₙ = a + (n − 1)d — for example, a₁₀ = 2 + 9 × 5 = 47 for the AP 2, 7, 12, …
Inverse application: set aₙ equal to the target and solve for n — for example, −81 = 21 + (n − 1)(−3) gives n = 35, so −81 is the 35th term.
Reconstruction: two term conditions give two equations; subtract to find d, then substitute to find a — for example, a₃ = 5 and a₇ = 9 give d = 1 and a = 3.
Membership test: if solving aₙ = target yields a non-integer n, the target is NOT a term — for example, n = 302/6 = 151/3 proves 301 is absent from 5, 11, 17, 23, …

recall_questions.answer:
Given: a = 2, d = 3, check if aₙ = 47.
Formula/Rule: aₙ = a + (n − 1)d. Set equal to 47 and solve for n.
Substitution: 47 = 2 + (n − 1) × 3.
Calculation:
  47 − 2 = (n − 1) × 3
  45 = (n − 1) × 3
  n − 1 = 15
  n = 16
Result: 47 is the 16th term of the AP. Since n = 16 is a positive integer, 47 is indeed a term of this AP.
recall_questions.prompt: An AP has first term a = 2 and common difference d = 3. Check whether 47 is a term of this AP. If yes, find its position n. Show all working.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: AP is 7, 13, 19, 25, … so a = 7, d = 13 − 7 = 6.
Formula/Rule: aₙ = a + (n − 1)d.

Part 1 — 20th term:
  a₂₀ = 7 + (20 − 1) × 6 = 7 + 19 × 6 = 7 + 114 = 121.
  The 20th term is 121.

Part 2 — Position of 205:
  Substitution: 205 = 7 + (n − 1) × 6.
  Calculation: 205 − 7 = (n − 1) × 6 → 198 = (n − 1) × 6 → n − 1 = 33 → n = 34.
  Result: 205 is the 34th term of the AP.
recall_questions.prompt: For the AP 7, 13, 19, 25, …, find the 20th term. Then determine which term of the AP is equal to 205. Show complete working.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: a = 121, d = 117 − 121 = −4. Find the first n such that aₙ < 0.
Formula/Rule: aₙ = a + (n − 1)d < 0.
Substitution: 121 + (n − 1)(−4) < 0.
Calculation:
  121 − 4(n − 1) < 0
  121 < 4(n − 1)
  n − 1 > 121/4 = 30.25
  n > 31.25
  Smallest integer n = 32.
Verification: a₃₂ = 121 + 31 × (−4) = 121 − 124 = −3 < 0 ✓
  a₃₁ = 121 + 30 × (−4) = 121 − 120 = 1 > 0 ✓ (still positive)
Result: The 32nd term, a₃₂ = −3, is the first negative term of this AP.

recall_questions.answer:
Terms of an AP occupy discrete positions 1, 2, 3, … — there is no 4.6th position in a sequence. If n turns out to be a non-integer positive number, it means the target value falls between two actual terms of the AP but is not itself a term.

Example: Consider the AP 2, 5, 8, 11, … (a = 2, d = 3). Check whether 20 is a term.
  aₙ = 20: 2 + (n − 1) × 3 = 20 → (n − 1) × 3 = 18 → n − 1 = 6 → n = 7. ✓ (integer — 20 is the 7th term)

Now check whether 21 is a term:
  2 + (n − 1) × 3 = 21 → (n − 1) × 3 = 19 → n − 1 = 19/3 → n = 19/3 + 1 = 22/3 ≈ 7.33. Not an integer.
  Correct conclusion: 21 is not a term of this AP. It lies between the 7th term (20) and the 8th term (23).

modules.detailed_summary: Module 2 derives and applies the nth term formula aₙ = a + (n − 1)d, enabling students to compute any term of an AP directly without iterating through all preceding terms. Segment M2.S3 first builds the formula from the pattern of repeated addition seen in Reena's salary sequence, then applies it in four distinct modes — forward computation, inverse position-finding, reconstruction from two known terms, and AP membership testing. The key algebraic insight that drives the module is the off-by-one structure: the coefficient of d is always (n − 1) because the first term requires zero additions. Once students master this, they can answer questions about APs of any length in a single substitution step, setting the stage for the sum formula in Module 3.

aₙ is also called the general term of the AP. If there are m terms in the AP, then aₘ represents the last term which is sometimes also denoted by l.
But n should be a positive integer (Why?). So, 301 is not a term of the given list of numbers.

Solving the pair of linear equations (1) and (2), we get
a = 3, d = 1
Hence, the required AP is 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, . . .
Therefore, the 35th term of the given AP is – 81.
Therefore, the 10th term of the given AP is 47.

modules.summary: Module 3 extends the nth term formula into advanced multi-step problems and introduces the sum formula Sₙ = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d], derived from Gauss's symmetric-pairing technique. Segment M3.S4 tackles harder nth term problems — counting terms satisfying a condition, finding a term from the end, and translating real-world situations (simple interest, flower beds) into AP calculations. Segment M3.S5 derives both sum formula forms, applies them to direct computation and to problems where Sₙ is known, introduces the aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁ relation, and shows how to sum sequences defined by an algebraic nth term expression. The unifying insight across both segments is that the same structural formula can be rearranged to solve for whichever of the four quantities {a, d, n, Sₙ} is unknown, making it a flexible algebraic tool rather than a one-direction computation.

topics.summary: The nth term formula is extended to count terms satisfying a divisibility condition (by setting aₙ equal to the last qualifying term and solving for n) and to find a term measured from the end of a finite AP, using the conversion forward position = (total terms) − (reverse position) + 1, or alternatively by reversing the AP to swap a and d.
topics.topic_name: Advanced nth Term Problems — Counting Terms, Reversing the AP, and Multi-Step Reasoning
topics.brief_summary: Advanced uses of aₙ = a + (n − 1)d include counting terms in a divisible-by-3 AP (30 two-digit numbers) and finding the 11th-from-last term via position conversion n − 11 + 1 = 15 or AP reversal.
topics.modified_chunk:
HOOK: The formula aₙ = a + (n − 1)d is flexible enough to handle two types of problems that initially appear different from the basic form: (1) counting how many terms in an AP satisfy a given condition, and (2) finding a term measured from the end rather than the beginning. Examples 7 and 8 develop each of these techniques.

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — Complete (counting terms satisfying a divisibility condition):

Example 7: How many two-digit numbers are divisible by 3?

Solution: The list of two-digit numbers divisible by 3 is:

12, 15, 18, . . . , 99

Is this an AP? Yes it is. Here, a = 12, d = 3, aₙ = 99.

As aₙ = a + (n – 1) d,
we have 99 = 12 + (n – 1) × 3
i.e., 87 = (n – 1) × 3
i.e., n – 1 = 87/3 = 29
i.e., n = 29 + 1 = 30

So, there are 30 two-digit numbers divisible by 3.

WHY THIS STEP? We treated the last term 99 as aₙ and solved for n. The result n = 30 is the count of terms, because term position equals term count in a complete, consecutive AP.

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — Partially faded (solve the main calculation yourself before reading the Alternative Solution):

Example 8: Find the 11th term from the last term (towards the first term) of the AP : 10, 7, 4, . . ., – 62.

Solution: Here, a = 10, d = 7 – 10 = – 3, l = – 62,
where l = a + (n – 1) d

To find the 11th term from the last term, we will find the total number of terms in the AP.

So, – 62 = 10 + (n – 1)(–3)
i.e., – 72 = (n – 1)(–3)
i.e., n – 1 = 24
or n = 25

So, there are 25 terms in the given AP.

The 11th term from the last term will be the 15th term. (Note that it will not be the 14th term. Why?)

So, a₁₅ = 10 + (15 – 1)(–3) = 10 – 42 = – 32
i.e., the 11th term from the last term is – 32.

Alternative Solution:
If we write the given AP in the reverse order, then a = – 62 and d = 3 (Why?)
So, the question now becomes finding the 11th term with these a and d.
So, a₁₁ = – 62 + (11 – 1) × 3 = – 62 + 30 = – 32
So, the 11th term, which is now the required term, is – 32.

WHY THIS STEP? The 11th term from the last is the (25 − 11 + 1) = 15th term from the first — not the 14th. This is because counting backwards from position 25, the 1st term from the last is position 25, the 2nd is position 24, and the 11th is position 25 − 11 + 1 = 15. The Alternative Solution avoids this adjustment by simply reversing the AP, which changes only the sign of d.

ERROR ALERT: A common mistake is subtracting 11 from 25 to get the 14th term, forgetting the +1 adjustment when converting between reverse-position and forward-position counting. Always use the formula: forward position = (total terms) − (reverse position) + 1.

CHECK: Verify the answer −32 using the Alternative Solution: starting from a = −62 and d = 3, confirm that a₁₁ = −62 + (11 − 1) × 3 = −32 ✓.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: Total terms n = 25, a = 3, d = 2. Find the 11th term from the last.
Formula/Rule: The kth term from the last of an AP with n terms = the (n − k + 1)th term from the first.
Substitution: 11th from last = (25 − 11 + 1)th from first = 15th term.
Calculation: a₁₅ = 3 + (15 − 1) × 2 = 3 + 14 × 2 = 3 + 28 = 31.
Result: The 11th term from the last is 31.
recall_questions.prompt: An AP has 25 terms, first term 3, and common difference 2. Using the formula aₙ = a + (n − 1)d, find the 11th term from the last. Show all steps.

recall_questions.answer:
Error: The student confused '11th from the last' with '11th from the first'. These refer to different terms. The 11th from the last counts backward from the final term.

Correct approach:
  The kth term from the last = the (n − k + 1)th term from the first.
  Here, k = 11 and n = 25.
  Position from first = 25 − 11 + 1 = 15.
  So the 11th from the last is the 15th term from the first: a₁₅ = a + 14d.

The student's formula a + 10d gives the 11th term from the first, not from the last. For an AP with 25 terms, these are entirely different positions (11th vs 15th from the beginning).
recall_questions.prompt: A student was asked to find the 11th term from the last of an AP with 25 terms, and wrote: '11th from last = 11th from first = a + 10d'. Identify the error and show the correct approach.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: a = 7, d = 10 − 7 = 3, last term l = 88.
Formula/Rule: aₙ = a + (n − 1)d. Set aₙ = 88 and solve for n.
Substitution: 88 = 7 + (n − 1) × 3.
Calculation:
  88 − 7 = (n − 1) × 3
  81 = (n − 1) × 3
  n − 1 = 27
  n = 28.
Verification: a₂₈ = 7 + 27 × 3 = 7 + 81 = 88 ✓.
Result: There are 28 terms in the AP 7, 10, 13, …, 88.

topics.brief_summary: Simple interest amounts (₹80, ₹160, ₹240, … with d = 80) and flower-bed row counts (23, 21, 19, …, 5 with d = −2) are modelled as APs, and aₙ = a + (n − 1)d is applied to find the 30-year interest (₹2400) and the number of rows (10).
topics.modified_chunk:
RECALL: The formula aₙ = a + (n − 1)d becomes a tool for real-world problem-solving when we translate a physical or financial situation into an AP, identify a, d, and the unknown, then solve. Every word problem of this type requires an explicit translation step before any algebra is written.

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — Complete (interest amounts forming an AP):

THE PROBLEM: A sum of ₹ 1000 is invested at 8% simple interest per year. Do the interest amounts at the end of each year form an AP? If so, find the interest at the end of 30 years.

WHAT'S THE SITUATION? Simple interest on a fixed principal grows by the same fixed amount each year — the interest is proportional to time, so consecutive yearly interest values differ by a constant.

WHAT DO WE KNOW?
- Principal P = ₹ 1000, rate R = 8% per year
- Simple Interest formula: SI = P × R × T / 100
- Interest at end of year 1 = ₹ (1000 × 8 × 1)/100 = ₹ 80
- Interest at end of year 2 = ₹ 160; interest at end of year 3 = ₹ 240

WHAT DO WE WANT TO FIND? Interest at the end of year 30, i.e., a₃₀.

TRANSLATE TO MATHS: The interest sequence is 80, 160, 240, . . . which is an AP with a = 80, d = 80.

SOLVE:
Example 9 Solution: We know that the formula to calculate simple interest is given by

Simple Interest = P×R×T/100

So, the interest at the end of the 1st year = ₹ (1000 × 8 × 1)/100 = ₹ 80
The interest at the end of the 2nd year = ₹ (1000 × 8 × 2)/100 = ₹ 160
The interest at the end of the 3rd year = ₹ (1000 × 8 × 3)/100 = ₹ 240

Similarly, we can obtain the interest at the end of the 4th year, 5th year, and so on.
So, the interest (in ₹) at the end of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, . . . years, respectively are

80, 160, 240, . . .

It is an AP as the difference between the consecutive terms in the list is 80, i.e., d = 80. Also, a = 80.

So, to find the interest at the end of 30 years, we shall find a₃₀.

Now, a₃₀ = a + (30 – 1) d = 80 + 29 × 80 = 2400

So, the interest at the end of 30 years will be ₹ 2400.

CHECK AGAINST THE SITUATION: ₹ 2400 = 8% of ₹ 1000 × 30 years = ₹ 80 × 30 = ₹ 2400. ✓ The formula and the direct calculation agree.

WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — Partially faded (write the AP and set up the equation yourself before reading the solution):

THE PROBLEM: In a flower bed, there are 23 rose plants in the first row, 21 in the second, 19 in the third, and so on. There are 5 rose plants in the last row. How many rows are there in the flower bed?

WHAT DO WE KNOW? a = 23, d = −2, aₙ = 5. We need to find n.

Example 10 Solution: The number of rose plants in the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, . . ., rows are:

23, 21, 19, . . ., 5

It forms an AP (Why?). Let the number of rows in the flower bed be n.

Then a = 23, d = 21 – 23 = – 2, aₙ = 5

As, aₙ = a + (n – 1) d
We have, 5 = 23 + (n – 1)(– 2)
i.e., – 18 = (n – 1)(– 2)
i.e., n = 10

So, there are 10 rows in the flower bed.

ERROR ALERT: Simple interest and compound interest appear similar but behave very differently as APs. Simple interest increases the interest value by the same rupee amount each year (constant addition → AP). Compound interest increases by a growing rupee amount each year (the amount multiplies by a factor → NOT an AP). This distinction applies directly to Question 1(iv) in Exercise 5.1 that you completed earlier.

CHECK: For Example 10, verify n = 10 by computing a₁₀ = 23 + (10 − 1)(−2) = 23 − 18 = 5 ✓. The 10th row indeed has 5 plants.

23, 21, 19, . . ., 5

It forms an AP (Why?). Let the number of rows in the flower bed be n.

Then a = 23, d = 21 – 23 = – 2, aₙ = 5

As, aₙ = a + (n – 1) d
We have, 5 = 23 + (n – 1)(– 2)
i.e., – 18 = (n – 1)(– 2)
i.e., n = 10

So, there are 10 rows in the flower bed.
concept_bullets: Simple interest on a fixed principal grows by the same rupee amount every year, forming an AP — for example, ₹1000 at 8% gives interests ₹80, ₹160, ₹240, … with a = 80 and d = 80.
The translation step for word problems is: identify what changes uniformly (the quantity forming the AP), name a and d, then apply aₙ = a + (n − 1)d — for example, a₃₀ = 80 + 29 × 80 = ₹2400.
Compound interest multiplies by a factor at each step (differences grow), so it does NOT form an AP — unlike simple interest where the annual interest increment is constant.
Counting rows in a decreasing AP: set aₙ equal to the last row count and solve for n — for example, 5 = 23 + (n − 1)(−2) gives n = 10 rows.
topics.detailed_summary: Real-world uniform-change situations — simple interest yielding annual interest amounts of ₹80, ₹160, ₹240, … and a flower bed with row counts 23, 21, 19, …, 5 — are translated into APs by identifying the first term a and constant increment d, then the nth term formula is applied to find the required term or the total count.
important_points: Simple Interest = P×R×T/100
It is an AP as the difference between the consecutive terms in the list is 80, i.e., d = 80. Also, a = 80.
So, the interest at the end of 30 years will be ₹ 2400.
So, there are 10 rows in the flower bed.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: Principal P = ₹ 5000, rate r = 5% per year. Simple interest each year = P × r/100 = 5000 × 5/100 = ₹ 250.
So the interest earned is the same every year: ₹ 250, ₹ 250, ₹ 250, …
This is an AP with a = 250 and d = 0 (constant sequence).

The total simple interest up to year n = 250n. This amount grows by ₹ 250 every year — a constant addition — confirming an AP.

Interest in the 8th year: a₈ = 250 + (8 − 1) × 0 = 250.
Result: The interest earned each year is ₹ 250. (The sequence of annual simple interest values is a constant AP with d = 0.)
recall_questions.prompt: A sum of ₹ 5000 is invested at simple interest of 5% per year. Show that the interest earned each year forms an AP, and find the interest in the 8th year.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: a = 30 (first row), d = −3 (3 fewer each row), aₙ = 3 (last row).
Formula/Rule: aₙ = a + (n − 1)d. Set equal to 3 and solve for n.
Substitution: 3 = 30 + (n − 1)(−3).
Calculation:
  3 − 30 = (n − 1)(−3)
  −27 = −3(n − 1)
  n − 1 = 9
  n = 10.
Verification: a₁₀ = 30 + 9 × (−3) = 30 − 27 = 3 ✓.
Result: There are 10 rows in the flower bed.
recall_questions.prompt: A flower bed has 30 rose plants in the first row, with each subsequent row having 3 fewer plants than the row before. The last row has 3 plants. How many rows are there in the flower bed? Show all steps.

recall_questions.answer:
Simple Interest (AP): Each year, interest earned = P × r/100 = a fixed amount. So cumulative totals grow by the same fixed amount every year. For P = ₹ 1000 at 10% per year: totals are ₹ 100, ₹ 200, ₹ 300, … — a constant difference of ₹ 100. This is an AP with d = 100.

Compound Interest (not AP): Interest in year 1 = P × r/100. But interest in year 2 = (P + interest from year 1) × r/100 — a larger base gives a larger interest. The amounts grow multiplicatively, not additively. For P = ₹ 1000 at 10%: cumulative totals after each year are ₹ 100, ₹ 210, ₹ 331, … Differences are ₹ 110, ₹ 121 — not constant.

Conclusion: Simple interest adds a fixed amount every year (constant difference → AP); compound interest multiplies by a fixed factor each year (growing difference → not AP).

concept_bullets: Given any three of {a, d, n, aₙ}, substitute into aₙ = a + (n − 1)d and solve for the fourth — for example, with a = 7, d = 3, n = 8 we compute aₙ = 7 + 7 × 3 = 28.

Membership test: solve aₙ = target for n; if n is not a positive integer, the target is absent — for example, −150 = 11 + (n − 1)(−3) gives n = 54.33, so −150 is not a term of 11, 8, 5, 2, …

Given: a = −5, d = −2 − (−5) = 3.

Part 1 — 20th term:
  a₂₀ = −5 + (20 − 1) × 3 = −5 + 57 = 52.
  The 20th term is 52.

Part 2 — Is 100 a term?
  Set aₙ = 100: −5 + (n − 1) × 3 = 100.
  (n − 1) × 3 = 105
  n − 1 = 35
  n = 36.
  Since n = 36 is a positive integer, 100 is the 36th term of the AP.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: a₅ = 22, a₁₅ = 62.
Formula/Rule: aₙ = a + (n − 1)d.
Substitution:
  Equation 1: a + 4d = 22
  Equation 2: a + 14d = 62
Calculation (subtract Eq. 1 from Eq. 2):
  (a + 14d) − (a + 4d) = 62 − 22
  10d = 40
  d = 4.
Substitute d = 4 into Equation 1:
  a + 4(4) = 22 → a + 16 = 22 → a = 6.
Verification: a₅ = 6 + 4 × 4 = 22 ✓ and a₁₅ = 6 + 14 × 4 = 62 ✓.
Result: First term a = 6, common difference d = 4.

Given: a₃ = 2000, a₇ = 2800. Fees form an AP with first term a and common difference d.

Equation 1: a + 2d = 2000
Equation 2: a + 6d = 2800

Subtract Eq. 1 from Eq. 2:
  4d = 800 → d = 200.
Substitute into Eq. 1:
  a + 400 = 2000 → a = 1600.

1st month fee = a = ₹ 1600.
12th month fee: a₁₂ = 1600 + 11 × 200 = 1600 + 2200 = ₹ 3800.

Verification: a₃ = 1600 + 2 × 200 = 2000 ✓; a₇ = 1600 + 6 × 200 = 2800 ✓.

Error: The student confused the 11th term from the last with the 11th term from the first. a + 10d is the 11th term from the first (position n = 11).

Correct method (from T7): The kth term from the last of an n-term AP is the (n − k + 1)th term from the first.
  Here, k = 11 and n = 25: position from first = 25 − 11 + 1 = 15.
  So the 11th term from the last = a₁₅ = a + 14d.

The formula a + 10d gives the wrong position because it treats 'from the last' identically to 'from the first'. The correct approach subtracts from the total number of terms and adds 1 to convert the backward count into a forward position.

topics.modified_chunk:
EX3 CONTEXT: Consider a mason laying tiles in a triangular section of a wall: the bottom row has 19 tiles, the next has 17, then 15, and so on. To find the total number of tiles, adding each row individually is tedious. There are 10 rows (the sequence ends at 1), so the total is 19 + 17 + 15 + . . . + 1 — ten numbers to add by hand. For even larger sequences — 21 terms, 50 terms, 100 terms — manual addition becomes impractical. This section derives a formula that replaces all that addition with a single computation.

5.4 Sum of First n Terms of an AP

Let us consider the situation again given in Section 5.1 in which Shakila put ₹ 100 into her daughter's money box when she was one year old, ₹ 150 on her second birthday, ₹ 200 on her third birthday and will continue in the same way. How much money will be collected in the money box by the time her daughter is 21 years old?

Here, the amount of money (in ₹) put in the money box on her first, second, third, fourth . . . birthday were respectively 100, 150, 200, 250, . . . till her 21st birthday. To find the total amount in the money box on her 21st birthday, we will have to write each of the 21 numbers in the list above and then add them up. Don't you think it would be a tedious and time consuming process? Can we make the process shorter? This would be possible if we can find a method for getting this sum. Let us see.

We consider the problem given to Gauss (about whom you read in Chapter 1), to solve when he was just 10 years old. He was asked to find the sum of the positive integers from 1 to 100. He immediately replied that the sum is 5050. Can you guess how did he do? He wrote:

S = 1 + 2 + 3 + . . . + 99 + 100

And then, reversed the numbers to write

S = 100 + 99 + . . . + 3 + 2 + 1

Adding these two, he got

2S = (100 + 1) + (99 + 2) + . . . + (3 + 98) + (2 + 99) + (1 + 100)
= 101 + 101 + . . . + 101 + 101  (100 times)

So, S = (100 × 101)/2 = 5050, i.e., the sum = 5050.

WHY THIS STEP? Writing S twice — once forward and once in reverse — is the key insight. When we add the two versions term by term, every corresponding pair sums to the same value (100 + 1 = 101). With 100 such pairs, the total is 100 × 101 = 10100, and dividing by 2 gives S. This pairing technique works for any AP, not just consecutive integers.

We will now use the same technique to find the sum of the first n terms of an AP:

a, a + d, a + 2d, . . .

The nth term of this AP is a + (n – 1) d. Let S denote the sum of the first n terms of the AP. We have

S = a + (a + d) + (a + 2d) + . . . + [a + (n – 1) d]   (1)

Rewriting the terms in reverse order, we have

S = [a + (n – 1) d] + [a + (n – 2) d] + . . . + (a + d) + a   (2)

On adding (1) and (2), term-wise. we get

2S = [2a + (n – 1)d] + [2a + (n – 1)d] + ... + [2a + (n – 1)d] + [2a + (n – 1)d]
(n times)

or, 2S = n [2a + (n – 1) d]  (Since, there are n terms)

or, S = n/2 [2a + (n – 1) d]

So, the sum of the first n terms of an AP is given by

S = n/2 [2a + (n – 1) d]

We can also write this as S = n/2 [a + a + (n – 1) d]

i.e., S = n/2 (a + aₙ)   (3)

Now, if there are only n terms in an AP, then aₙ = l, the last term.
From (3), we see that

S = n/2 (a + l)   (4)

WHY THIS STEP? Two forms of the sum formula now exist. Use S = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d] when you know a and d but not the last term. Use S = n/2 (a + l) when you know the first and last terms but not d. Both are equivalent; choose the one that avoids extra calculation.

This form of the result is useful when the first and the last terms of an AP are given and the common difference is not given.

Now we return to the question that was posed to us in the beginning. The amount of money (in Rs) in the money box of Shakila's daughter on 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th birthday, . . ., were 100, 150, 200, 250, . . ., respectively.

This is an AP. We have to find the total money collected on her 21st birthday, i.e., the sum of the first 21 terms of this AP.

Here, a = 100, d = 50 and n = 21. Using the formula:

S = n/2 [2a + (n-1) d],

we have S = 21/2 [2 × 100 + (21 – 1) × 50]
= 21/2 [200 + 1000]
= 21/2 × 1200 = 12600

So, the amount of money collected on her 21st birthday is ₹ 12600.

Hasn't the use of the formula made it much easier to solve the problem?

We also use Sₙ in place of S to denote the sum of first n terms of the AP. We write S₂₀ to denote the sum of the first 20 terms of an AP. The formula for the sum of the first n terms involves four quantities S, a, d and n. If we know any three of them, we can find the fourth.

Remark: The nth term of an AP is the difference of the sum to first n terms and the sum to first (n – 1) terms of it, i.e., aₙ = Sₙ – Sₙ₋₁.

WHY THIS STEP? This Remark creates a powerful bridge between the sum formula and the nth term formula: if you know the sum formula Sₙ, you can recover any individual term by computing Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁. This is particularly useful in Exercise 5.3 questions where Sₙ is given as an expression in n and you are asked to find individual terms.

ERROR ALERT: When a problem states the sum Sₙ as an algebraic expression (e.g., Sₙ = 4n − n²), the nth term is NOT the expression itself. It is aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁. Many students mistakenly equate Sₙ with aₙ. Always subtract Sₙ₋₁ to isolate the individual term.

Let us consider some examples.

recall_questions.answer:
Formula 1: Sₙ = n/2 × [2a + (n − 1)d], where a = first term, d = common difference, n = number of terms.

Formula 2: Sₙ = n/2 × (a + l), where a = first term, l = last term (aₙ), n = number of terms.

Formula 2 is more convenient when both the first and last terms are known. Formula 1 is used when a and d are known but the last term is not given. The two formulas are equivalent: substituting l = a + (n − 1)d into Formula 2 gives Formula 1.
recall_questions.prompt: State the two equivalent formulas for the sum of the first n terms of an AP. Define every variable used.

recall_questions.answer:
Gauss pairing: Write the sum S forward and backward, then add the two rows term by term.

For 1, 2, 3, …, 100:
  S = 1 + 2 + 3 + … + 99 + 100
  S = 100 + 99 + 98 + … + 2 + 1
  2S = (1 + 100) + (2 + 99) + … + (100 + 1) = 100 pairs, each equal to 101.
  2S = 100 × 101 = 10100
  S = 5050.

In general, every pair (aₖ + aₙ₋ₖ₊₁) equals a + l (first term + last term). There are n such pairs when we write the sum twice, so 2Sₙ = n × (a + l), giving Sₙ = n/2 × (a + l). This is the Gauss pairing principle.
recall_questions.prompt: Using the Gauss pairing method, explain why Sₙ = n/2 × (a + l). Illustrate with the AP 1, 2, 3, …, 100.

recall_questions.answer:
Given: a = 5, d = 8 − 5 = 3, n = 20.
Formula/Rule: Sₙ = n/2 × [2a + (n − 1)d].
Substitution: S₂₀ = 20/2 × [2(5) + (20 − 1)(3)].
Calculation:
  S₂₀ = 10 × [10 + 19 × 3]
  S₂₀ = 10 × [10 + 57]
  S₂₀ = 10 × 67
  S₂₀ = 670.
Result: The sum of the first 20 terms of the AP is 670.
